  of it.

```python
import marrow as ma
from marrow import col, lit

(ma.read_parquet("orders.parquet")
   .filter(col("price") > lit(15))
   .aggregate(by=["region"], total=("sum", "price"))
   .order_by(("total", "descending"))
   .head(10)
   .optimize()
   .collect())
```

::::

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Eager Python

Names follow PyArrow's. Each call runs its kernel straight away.

```python
import marrow as ma

batch = ma.record_batch({
    "region": ma.array(["east", "west", "east"]),
    "price":  ma.array([10, 20, 30]),
})

hot = ma.compute.greater(batch.column("price"), ma.array([15, 15, 15]))
ma.compute.filter(batch.column("price"), hot)
```

## Lazy Python

Describe the query first and run it with `collect()`. Add `optimize()` to let
the plan rewriter push filters down and prune columns before it runs.

```python
import marrow as ma
from marrow import col, lit

ma.read_parquet("orders.parquet") \
  .filter(col("price") > lit(15)) \
  .aggregate(by=["region"], total=("sum", "price")) \
  .optimize() \
  .collect()
```

## Compiled Mojo

Column types are fixed when the query is compiled, so an expression can fuse
into a single loop, and kernels the query never uses are not linked in. The
filter threshold and the input path stay command-line arguments.

```mojo
from marrow.dtypes import field, int64, string
from marrow.expr import QueryCli, col, scan
from marrow.schema import schema

def main() raises:
    var cli = QueryCli(String("orders"))
    var min_amount = cli.param(String("min-amount"), int64, default=Int64(0))
    cli.argument(String("src"))

    if cli.parse():
        var sch = schema(
            [field("id", int64), field("amount", int64), field("name", string)]
        )
        cli.run(
            scan(cli.get(String("src")), sch^).filter(
                col("amount", int64) >= min_amount
            )
        )
```

```bash
$ marrow compile query.mojo -o orders
$ ./orders orders.parquet --min-amount 250
```

Building takes a minute or two, so this suits a query you run many times, not
one you are still shaping. `--bundle` copies the executable together with the
runtime libraries it loads, for running it on another machine.

:::

```{=html}
<div class="mr-section-head">
  <span class="mr-eyebrow">Where it fits</span>
  <h2 class="mr-section-title">Next to the tools you already use</h2>
  <p>Each of these is more complete and better tested than marrow. The right
  column is what marrow offers anyway.</p>
</div>
```

| | What it is | What marrow offers |
|---|---|---|
| **PyArrow** | Python bindings to Arrow C++, the reference implementation | Similar method names, and arrays pass between the two without copying their buffers |
| **Polars / DuckDB** | Mature query engines with far broader features | A fixed query compiled into its own executable. No benchmark results are published yet, so no speed claims |
| **arrow-rs / DataFusion** | Arrow and a query engine in Rust, the closest relatives in design | Its IPC and C Data output is tested against arrow-rs, C++ and Go in Arrow's integration suite |
| **Mojo** | The language marrow is written in | Arrow arrays, Parquet and a query engine for Mojo programs; a few element-wise kernels can also run on a GPU behind a build flag |

::: {.callout-note}
## How correctness is checked
A corpus of 278 SQL queries whose expected answers come from DuckDB, never from
marrow: 215 run and match, and 63 wait on features marrow does not have yet.
Arrow's own integration suite round-trips IPC files and
C Data with the C++, Rust and Go implementations, skipping the layouts marrow
does not implement (unions, views, run-end encoding, extension types). See
[Status & limitations](reference/status.qmd) for the full list.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "../python")   # the built extension
import marrow as ma
from marrow import col, lit
```

Build arrays from Python data. The type is inferred, and `None` marks a null:

```{python}
ages   = ma.array([25, 35, 45, None, 55])
names  = ma.array(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve"])
salary = ma.array([70_000, 90_000, 110_000, 50_000, 130_000])

print(ages)
print(names)
```

Kernels are vectorized and null-aware; a null in either operand gives a null:

```{python}
print("next year:", ma.compute.add(ages, ma.array([1] * 5)))
print("over 40:  ", ma.compute.greater(ages, ma.array([40] * 5)))
```

Assemble columns into a `RecordBatch`, then query it lazily:

```{python}
people = ma.record_batch({"age": ages, "name": names, "salary": salary})

(ma.memtable(people)
   .filter(col("salary") > lit(60_000))
   .aggregate(headcount=("count", "salary"), payroll=("sum", "salary"))
   .collect()
   .to_pylist())
```

Arrays implement the Arrow PyCapsule interface, so PyArrow takes them without
copying the buffers, and marrow takes PyArrow's the same way:

```{python}
import pyarrow as pa
pa_ages = pa.array(ages)          # marrow → PyArrow, no copy
back    = ma.array(pa_ages)       # PyArrow → marrow, no copy
print(pa_ages.type, "|", len(back))
```
